headline: Russian Starlink rival Rassvet satellites fail to reach orbit, two falling back to Earth
summary: A second batch of 16 Rassvet satellites launched in mid-June have failed to reach their target operational altitudes, with some already decaying.
details: The entire second batch of 16 Russian Rassvet satellites, intended as a rival to Elon Musk's Starlink, has failed to reach their target operational altitudes of 870 kilometers. Many of these satellites ended up between 300 and 400 kilometers, and two are already experiencing orbital decay.

Developed by Bureau 1440, Russia aims to expand the Rassvet constellation to 900 satellites by 2035. However, this recent failure casts doubt on their ability to meet even interim targets, such as providing 250 operational satellites by 2027.

The first batch of 16 Rassvet satellites also faced issues, with only 12 reaching their anticipated altitudes and one already dropping out of orbit. Operating at lower altitudes requires more fuel and reduces satellite lifespan.

Currently, Rassvet offers only two brief connectivity windows per day over Ukraine. Russia requires an estimated 200 to 300 fully operational satellites for stable 24/7 connectivity, a goal that appears increasingly distant.

headline_marked: Pangram AI detector [[claims to be the gold standard]] for identifying AI-generated text
headline: Pangram AI detector claims to be the gold standard for identifying AI-generated text
summary: This AI startup, with just 24 employees and $13 million in funding, is making waves by flagging AI content in books, news articles, and even Substack posts.
details: Pangram, a 24-employee startup, has raised $13 million and claims its AI detection technology is the best available. The company uses methods like 'synthetic mirroring' and 'hard negative mining' to identify AI-generated text, providing a percentage score for its findings.

The startup gained significant attention after flagging Mia Ballard's self-published novel "Shy Girl" as 78% AI-generated, leading Hachette to cancel its traditional publication. Similar accusations followed, with Pangram scoring The New York Times' Modern Love column at 100% AI-generated and a thriller sold for $2.4 million at 97% AI-generated.

Substack recently announced it is integrating Pangram's technology to allow readers to quickly assess the potential AI use in articles. However, some authors and publishing experts express skepticism and even anger towards AI detection software, viewing it as potentially as harmful as AI generation itself.

Pangram's CEO, Max Spero, co-founded the company after working at Google on FLoC and at autonomous car company Nuro. He and co-founder Bradley Emi saw an opportunity to address the growing challenge of distinguishing human writing from AI-generated content after the launch of ChatGPT.

Despite its recent success and a $9 million funding round, Pangram faces competition from other AI detection companies like Originality.ai, GPTZero, and Turnitin. The core question remains: how much can Pangram's detection capabilities be trusted in an increasingly AI-driven content landscape?
